sources.news_title: Bonfire of the Neocons: The MAGA Finger-Pointing Begins
sources.text:
Good afternoon from Washington, where foie gras is now illegal and the local Stasi is going door-to-door to check that every citizen has downloaded Bluesky.
The town, one of the bluest in the country, is in a state of stunned ecstasy as it struggles to process the mind-bending midterm election results. Democrats won the House, the Senate, and a majority of governorships, penetrating deep into historically red strongholds like Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina. During a book party for Sophia Bush at The Jefferson hotel on Wednesday night, the actor nearly cried as she delivered a toast to the results—and to her new bestseller.
On the right, the finger-pointing has already begun. In this edition of Party Animals, you can read my dispatch from a night out with the DC Republicans in mourning and the Democrats celebrating in cocktail-fueled delirium. Plus, a MAGA civil war reignites over Iran, with Vice President JD Vance already wading into the factional fight that could determine the future of the party.
Also mentioned in this issue: Marc Thiessen, Curt Mills, Darline Graham, Ken Paxton, Greg Abbott, James Talarico, Annie Andrews, Mark Mitchell, Matt Walsh, and more.
Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be drowned in cocktail-fueled delirium. Praise will be run as a Democrat south of the Mason-Dixon Line.
IN THE LOOP
The morning after the generational Republican midterm collapse that Party Animals is dubbing Blue Tuesday, JD Vance put on his political-analyst cap. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a lengthy X post. “The president himself said so last night.”
Never mind that Vance’s referenced war is one that his own administration started and is currently presiding over. Vance has often tried to cast himself as an outside observer of the Trump administration, its preeminent reply guy on social media and podcasts—a clever, if often ludicrous, pose for the vice president.
The Vance post was the highest-level opening salvo in a civil war that had been brewing for some time. It erupted into the open on Tuesday night as the results began to spell doom for Republicans and the blame started flying with velocity. The internecine battle is between the “America First” faction of the Trump movement and those who have supported the war in Iran, the latter labeled by detractors—with a sneer—as neocons.
“The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” wrote Matt Walsh in a post on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.” As the dire results came down, even some on the right who had cheered on the war came to see, in the cold glow of their screens, the political devastation it had wrought. “Iran War is clearly catastrophically unpopular and has to end,” posted Will Chamberlain, who had spent the last few months loudly dismissing the war’s critics as subliterate simpletons.
On social media, MAGA luminaries shared a screenshot of an infamous op-ed written by Iran war booster Marc Thiessen, whose headline confidently claimed earlier this year: “There is no US downside to striking the Iranian regime.” Fox host Mark Levin lashed out at critics blasting his support for the war, insisting it had nothing to do with the results. Reality would seem to differ. One NBC News exit poll found that 74% of voters said Iran was a “crucial or major factor in how they voted.”
“It was the Iran war, stupid,” said Curt Mills, the executive director of The American Conservative, in an interview with Party Animals. Speaking about Thiessen and Levin, Mills was unsparing: “Professional liars. Professional liars. Not analysts, not honest people, and, honestly, not very invested in the future of the country.”
I asked Mills, who praised Vance’s statement, if it was not strange for the vice president to speak out against the administration while serving in it. “What option does he really have if he wants to keep his job, stop the war, and maybe run for president? I mean, it is strange. It is unprecedented in some ways,” he said. “Is it working? Maybe.”
The Headline
In restaurants and barrooms across the capital, the ruling party’s apparatchiks watched and agonized as Democrats mounted a historic midterms rout.
Required Reading
The How: The Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey and colleagues have the definitive account of how Trump lost the midterms for Republicans, packed with genuinely shocking reporting that reveals exactly what went wrong at each turn.
Rockstud the Vote: My colleague José Criales-Unzueta trained his gimlet eye on a photo posted by Free Press reporter Olivia Reingold from a Democratic election night party in Michigan and found some suspicious discrepancies in the leather straps of a smoking heel.
Ballroom Blues: Read Shawn McCreesh’s New York Times dispatch from Trump’s strange walk of shame around the White House ballroom construction site the morning after the midterms. “Inside his concrete chrysalis,” McCreesh writes, “everything was still beautiful.” 💔
Department of (Deeply Unpopular) War: Amid a flurry of anonymous quotes from Trump officials and allies laying blame for the midterms on Pete Hegseth, the president tells Jonathan Karl of ABC News that he’s standing by his defense secretary—for now, at least.
Of Mics and Men: In the wake of Patrick Bet-David’s election night stream, Vanity Fair’s Dan Adler has a biting eulogy for the manosphere: “Donald Trump’s 2024 tour of the Joe Rogan–dominated podcast circuit heralded the makings of a new mainstream media. But in the MAGA midterm wreckage, the idea of the manosphere as a political force has shattered.”
A Few Good Streamers: VF’s Abigail Sylvor Greenberg spoke with Hasan Piker and his lawyer, who promised that Piker’s $75 million defamation lawsuit against Scott Jennings is only the beginning.
Russell Brand trial: The star comedian turned right-wing podcast lounge lizard was found guilty in a London court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Musk in the barrel: Elon Musk, who just torched nearly half a billion dollars in an effort to keep Republicans in power, now faces the wrath of Democrats. The New York Times has a handy guide to the coming storm. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Senator Ed Markey.

sources.news_title: The Iran war cost Republicans the midterms: A political price America could not afford
sources.text:
The results of the November 2026 midterm elections have delivered a painful political message to the Trump administration: Americans are increasingly unwilling to support a foreign war at the expense of their economic security. Vice President J.D. Vance appears to have acknowledged that reality, openly blaming the war with Iran for the Republican Party’s disappointing electoral performance. In a November 4 post on X, Vance declared, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.” His remarks suggest that the administration’s foreign policy decisions may have become a significant political liability for the Republican Party.
The election results underscore the scale of the Republican setback. Democrats reportedly flipped seven Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas, while the outcomes in Alaska and Mississippi remained uncertain. Democrats also appeared poised to secure a substantial majority in the House of Representatives, with projections approaching 260 seats. Although several races were still awaiting final results, the broader political message was difficult to ignore: a considerable number of voters who supported Donald Trump and J.D. Vance in 2024 chose Democratic candidates in 2026.
Perhaps the most revealing aspect of this political shift is that it was not simply a matter of Democratic voters becoming more enthusiastic or Republican supporters staying home. According to Vance, the central problem was that voters who had previously supported Trump and Vance changed their political allegiance. This development should concern Republican strategists far more than ordinary electoral fluctuations. When a governing party begins losing the confidence of its own electoral coalition, the problem is no longer merely about campaign messaging; it reflects a deeper disconnect between political leadership and public expectations.
The war in Iran appears to have been a major factor behind that disconnect. According to NBC exit polling, only 26 percent of voters considered the conflict a minor factor or no factor at all in their voting decisions. Furthermore, 63 percent said the Trump administration had made the wrong decision by taking military action against Iran. Among those who disapproved, 82 percent voted Democratic, compared with just 16 percent who supported Republican candidates. These figures suggest that opposition to the war extended beyond traditional Democratic constituencies and reached voters who might otherwise have remained loyal to the Republican Party.
However, the political consequences of the conflict cannot be separated from its economic impact. For ordinary Americans, foreign policy is not an abstract debate about military strategy or geopolitical influence. It becomes personal when families struggle to afford gasoline, groceries, transportation, and other basic necessities. An October Gallup poll identified gasoline prices as a major concern for 42 percent of voters, while Pew Research found that the economy remained a leading voting issue for both Republicans and Democrats. In other words, Americans were judging the administration not only by its international decisions but also by how those decisions affected their everyday lives.
The economic consequences of the Iran conflict have been particularly significant because of the strategic importance of the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most critical energy shipping routes. Disruptions to maritime traffic through this narrow passage contributed to higher energy costs, pushing the national average gasoline price from approximately $2.98 per gallon before the war to around $4.27 by October-a reported increase of roughly 43 percent. Diesel prices reportedly climbed by approximately 68 percent. Such increases do not remain confined to fuel stations. Higher transportation and agricultural costs place additional pressure on farmers, ranchers, manufacturers, retailers, and ultimately consumers. The result is a wider inflationary burden on households already struggling with the cost of living.
This is where the administration’s political calculations may have gone fundamentally wrong. A government can justify military action through national security arguments, strategic interests, or regional stability. But those explanations become increasingly difficult to defend politically when citizens see no clear endpoint to the conflict while their household expenses continue to rise. Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 largely expected a government focused on domestic prosperity, economic stability, and an America First agenda. For many of these voters, an expensive and prolonged foreign conflict may have appeared to contradict those promises.
Vance’s post-election remarks also point to another uncomfortable issue for the Republican leadership: the need to reconsider its broader foreign policy priorities, including America’s relationship with Israel. According to Vance’s account of a pollster’s findings, some former Trump voters indicated that ending the Iran war, addressing inflation, prioritizing American interests, and changing the country’s relationship with Israel could influence their willingness to return to the Republican camp. Whether Republican leaders agree with these demands or not, dismissing them would be a serious political mistake. Voters are increasingly demanding accountability for foreign policy decisions and questioning whether international commitments are consistent with America’s domestic priorities.
Ultimately, the 2026 midterm results should serve as a warning that electoral victories do not grant political leaders unlimited public support. Americans may accept difficult decisions when they believe those decisions serve a clear national interest. But they are far less likely to support policies that appear to bring escalating costs, economic uncertainty, and an open-ended military commitment without a convincing strategy for success.
The central question facing the Trump administration is therefore not simply how to recover from an electoral defeat. It is whether the administration is prepared to reconsider the policies that contributed to that defeat. If the Iran war has weakened public confidence, increased economic pressure, and alienated voters who once supported the Republican agenda, continuing along the same path could deepen the political damage.
As Vance himself questioned, was the war worth potentially losing control of the Senate for the next six years? That question captures the political dilemma facing the Republican Party. More importantly, it raises a question that extends beyond party politics: should America’s foreign policy ambitions come at the expense of the economic security and priorities of its own citizens?
The message from the ballot box is unmistakable. Americans want affordable living, economic stability, responsible leadership, and a foreign policy that puts their national interests first. If Washington fails to understand that message, the political consequences of the Iran war may extend well beyond the 2026 midterms.
Editorial note: This article is based on the material and source links you provided. Election figures, polling results, and economic statistics have been retained as reported in that material and have not been independently fact-checked.

sources.news_title: JD Vance makes his post-midterms move
sources.text:
JD Vance makes his post-midterms move
By pivoting away from Trump on Iran, has the vice president set the tone for the next two years?
Just 24 hours after his party’s midterm drubbing, Vice President JD Vance offered a pointed diagnosis of why MAGA lost: frustration over the Iran war. Despite couching his critique with brief genuflections toward Trump, Vance’s lengthy missive about why Republicans lost, shared yesterday on X, has been taken by some as a deliberate schism point between himself and the administration he ostensibly helps lead. With two years left of the Trump White House and a presumptive presidential run of his own after that, Vance seems set on not allowing this week’s losses to limit his political future.
‘Astonishing, if implicit, rebuke’
Vance’s statement represents a “striking acknowledgment” from a sitting vice president that his own administration’s “handling” of the Iran war has “become a political liability for Republicans,” said Politico, even as Trump himself has “defended the approach.” The “blunt assessment” comes as “speculation mounts over his own political future,” said Fox News. Vance’s remarks signify a “shift in his public assessment of the war’s consequences” after “previously defending aspects of the administration’s military campaign.”
While Vance had “expressed some reluctance” in the early days of Trump’s Iran war plans, the vice president ultimately embraced the “spineless sycophantism we’ve come to expect,” said The New Republic. After the Democrats’ seismic midterm performance, however, Vance “promptly threw the president under the bus.” The veep’s “astonishing, if implicit, rebuke” of a president he has backed “consistently and unequivocally for years” suggests the GOP is entering an era of “competing factions” that “more openly jockey for influence,” said HuffPost.
The Week
Escape your echo chamber. Get the facts behind the news, plus analysis from multiple perspectives.
Sign up for The Week's Free Newsletters
Join more than 350,000 subscribers and keep yourself informed with a selection of The Week’s most interesting, enlightening and entertaining stories - plus daily puzzles.
‘Better late than never’
Trump detractors have “delighted in watching the infighting,” said Mediaite. Some Republicans have already embraced Vance’s pivot, including outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a frequent critic of Trump’s foreign policy. “Better late than never,” said Massie, asserting he had been “right about everything” in response to Vance’s post on X.
When asked about whether the Iran war should be blamed for Republicans’ loss in the midterms, Trump “essentially agreed with Vance,” said HuffPost. Vance’s critique is “largely true” because the war “drove the gasoline up a little,” said Trump to reporters, per The Associated Press. However, he added, “if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”

Rafi Schwartz has worked as a politics writer at The Week since 2022, where he covers elections, Congress and the White House. He was previously a contributing writer with Mic focusing largely on politics, a senior writer with Splinter News, a staff writer for Fusion's news lab, and the managing editor of Heeb Magazine, a Jewish life and culture publication. Rafi's work has appeared in Rolling Stone, GOOD and The Forward, among others.

sources.news_title: J.D. Vance Is Going to Pretend He Doesn’t Work for Trump
sources.text:
Once upon a time, James David Vance not only understood what Donald Trump was all about but was willing to say it out loud. “Mr. Trump is unfit for our nation’s highest office,” he wrote in an New York Times op-ed in April 2016, a couple months before the release of his memoir Hillbilly Elegy. “I’m going to vote third party because I can’t stomach Trump,” he said on NPR that August. “I’m a ‘Never Trump’ guy. I never liked him,” he told Charlie Rose two months later. “Trump makes people I care about afraid. Immigrants, Muslims, etc. Because of this I find him reprehensible,” he wrote on social media on the eve of the election, around the same time he suggested he believed Trump had committed sexual assault. “Trump is a moral disaster,” he told a friend in the summer of 2017. In case none of that was blunt enough, made his feelings pretty clear when he described the guy as “America’s Hitler.” He also liked a post — the ultimate 21st-century endorsement! — featuring a photo of Trump and O.J. Simpson with the caption, “Here is an old picture of one of USA’s most hated, villainous, douchey celebs. Also in picture: OJ Simpson.”
Yet fast-forward a few years and Vance started singing a very different tune, one that went something like “I will sell my spine, every last bit of dignity, and anything that’s not nailed down to the floor to be vice-president.” Of course, no one aspires to be just vice-president — they see it as a stepping stone to the ultimate job in politics. And in Vance’s mind, he obviously believed hitching his wagon to a guy he once likened to a genocidal maniac was worth it so long as he could ride that thing all the way to the Oval Office.
But sad trombone for J.D.! Because after the events of Tuesday, wherein voters repudiated Donald Trump and the GOP in a historic flogging that pundits have run out of words to describe, his chances of becoming president in 2028 appear to be rapidly dwindling. Luckily, though, he’s got a plan. And the plan, it seems, is to disavow and distance himself from unpopular things his boss has done in office, starting with the war in Iran. In a 600-plus-word tweet published Wednesday morning, Vance told followers “The reason we lost is the war.”
According to some reports, the White House was aware of in advance, and fine with Vance’s post. According to another, he went somewhat rogue.
Complicating things is the fact that Trump told reporters he thought Vance’s post was “good,” though, to be fair, it’s also entirely possible he neither read it nor has been told what it said. (He does, after all, have an aide whose entire job is to keep him in a bubble of delusion.) And there’s the fact that he said he would not have done anything different re: the war. Furthermore, there seemed to be hints of tension when Trump mused to reporters that maybe the VP “won’t run” for president.
Should Vance continue to try to distance himself from Trump’s wildly unpopular policies, it seems more than a little likely that the president will completely turn on him, which has long been his m.o. (Whether or not he goes full Pence on his second VP remains to be seen.) But even if Vance doesn’t have to worry about the wrath of his boss, the question remains whether or not his weaselly attempts to separate himself from the administration in the eyes of 2028 will work. And the answer, according to some people, is absolutely not. “It’s possible for him to modestly differentiate himself,” a Vance ally with ties to the White House told Politico. “But there’s no way he can totally separate. He’s still Trump’s vice president. This is still a Trump administration war. They’re still both unpopular. He’s not as unpopular as Trump but he’s unpopular.” Or, as one House Republican put it, “I think he’s done.”

sources.news_title: JD Vance’s stunning act of disloyalty
VP Vance signals Iran war main reason GOP lost midterms; new voter poll data sheds insight
sources.text:
VP Vance signals Iran war main reason GOP lost midterms; new voter poll data sheds insight
WASHINGTON (TNND) — Republicans’ losses in the 2026 midterm elections are fueling a new round of finger-pointing inside the party, with Vice President JD Vance arguing the war with Iran was the decisive factor.
In a lengthy social media post Wednesday, Vance shared his thoughts on the 2026 midterm elections, which saw Democrats regain the majority in both chambers by flipping dozens of House seats and, as of Thursday night, seven seats in the Senate. Vance wrote, “The reason we lost is the war.” He added, “Everyone knows why we lost and any honest conversation about where we go from here must start here.”
President Donald Trump addressed Vance’s comments Wednesday, saying, “Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little, but short term.”
Trump also defended the decision to launch the conflict, saying, “But at the same time, if I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again because long term it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
New Fox News voter poll data showed the Iran war was a major issue for voters, particularly in the seven states where Democrats picked up Senate seats. When asked, “Thinking about your vote for Congress, how important to you was the war in Iran?” 73% of more than 2,000 Texas respondents said it was crucial or a major factor. In Kansas, where Democrats won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since the 1930s, the poll showed similar numbers, with 73% giving the same response. In Michigan, a state Democrats defended, the identical percentage said the war was top of mind.
Former White House director of speechwriting Marc Thiessen criticized Vance’s post, calling it “disloyal to the president.” While appearing on Fox News, Thiessen said, “I didn't see Vice President Vance say it was the right thing to do. I didn't see him say Donald Trump is one of the most courageous presidents in my lifetime because he took this very difficult political decision and put the country ahead of his own political interests.”
Meanwhile, the DSA said ending the war in Iran is a top priority as dozens of its candidates prepare to assume office, including over half a dozen elected at the federal level. Megan Romer told Fox News Wednesday, “So, ending the war with Iran is going to be a primary goal.”
As of Thursday night, Democrats were still waiting to see whether they flipped two more Senate seats in Alaska and Mississippi, or whether Republicans held those states.

sources.news_title: Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Midterms Wipeout
sources.text:
Vance Blames Iran War for GOP Midterms Wipeout
In a stunning statement, the U.S. vice president veered sharply from Trump’s defense of the war.
U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.
U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance on Wednesday offered an extraordinarily frank assessment of why he believes Republicans got clobbered in the 2026 midterm elections. He blamed the Iran war.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said on X.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
It’s not often that a sitting vice president comes out so forcefully against a defining policy decision made by his boss—especially when that boss is as notorious for punishing perceived disloyalty as U.S. President Donald Trump is.
But Vance, who is widely expected to be interested in running for president in 2028, appears to have calculated that the political cost of continuing to defend the Iran war outweighs the potential risk of drawing Trump’s ire.
In the lead-up to elections, polling consistently showed that the Iran war was unpopular among voters and that the cost of living was their top concern.
As Vance noted, Trump himself has acknowledged that the Iran war was a “piece” of what contributed to the historic defeat. But the president remains unapologetic about starting the war.
“I did the right thing. I would have done it again,” Trump told the Wall Street Journal.
Trump also blamed the quality of Republican candidates on the ballot, stating that some could’ve been “better.” In a separate interview with Fox News, Trump acknowledged voter discontentment over the war’s economic consequences, including high gas prices, but suggested the pain at the pump was worth it in the long run.
“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really, probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline,” Trump said. “And, you know, I understand that. I don’t agree with it, and I would say to people, you know, ‘It’s a short-term problem but for long-term gain.’”
But Trump and Vance have never done a particularly good job of selling the Iran war to the American people. Since the very beginning, the administration has presented muddled and often contradictory explanations for why the United States needed to launch a full-scale war on Iran in February.
Even in his final speech on the eve of the election, Trump undermined the war’s main justification by saying that Iran’s nuclear program had already been destroyed by U.S. military action last summer.
“I hope people realize that when they go into the voting booth, because we had to stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon. If, if we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way. The whole world would be a different place, so we’ve stopped that. We stopped that a year ago with those beautiful B-2 bombers, which hit every single mark, and just put hundreds of tons of rock on top of everything,” Trump said.
Vance is believed to have strongly opposed the war behind closed doors; yet he outwardly maintained support for it. It seems that American voters’ unequivocal rejection of the war has convinced him that he no longer has to pretend.
John Haltiwanger is a staff writer at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @jchaltiwanger.bsky.social X: @jchaltiwanger

The Republican Party's No. 2 has zeroed in on what he sees as the driving issue behind the GOP's bruising midterm loss. Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday publicly pinned the GOP's congressional collapse on the war with Iran, reports the New York Times, saying backers of the war must face the possibility they traded away control of Congress for "years." His comments came in a lengthy social media post:
- "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
His comments followed a nationwide vote that handed Democrats the House and Senate in what was widely seen as a rejection of how Trump has managed both the war and the economy. Trump, speaking to the Times on Tuesday night, stood by his decision to launch the Iran campaign, calling it necessary "for the country and the world." Axios notes that neither the White House nor Vance's office responded to requests for comment.

sources.news_title: Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us." - The Thinking Conservative News
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance on X
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was “composition”—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up.
So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we’re going to shock the world? “No,” he told me. “We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us.”
Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.
There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true.
But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.
Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:
- End the war
- Focus on cost of living/inflation
- Put America First
- Change our relationship to Israel
Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)
In the next few months, there’s going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you.
The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.
If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.
But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.
I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.

sources.news_title: Vance repudiates Iran war after US electoral defeat
JD Vance Criticizes Trump’s War in Iran in Sharp Rebuke
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance delivered a blunt rebuke of President Donald Trump’s war in Iran on Wednesday as he considers his political future and a potential 2028 presidential campaign.
In an extended post on X, Vance sharply assessed the Republican Party’s election losses, arguing that the conflict in Iran played a central role. He also appealed to GOP voters to give the MAGA movement another opportunity to regain momentum.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote.
He challenged supporters of the military action to acknowledge the political consequences of urging the United States into another conflict in the Middle East.
“If you want to argue that it was worth it—that losing the Senate for the next six years was a price worth paying—then make that case. Say it was a cost worth bearing. Whether people agree or disagree, at least that would be honest,” he said.
Vance published the message shortly before his motorcade reached the White House, where he was scheduled to attend private meetings.
Trump, meanwhile, had withdrawn from public view at the White House for a series of private policy discussions. No public appearances were listed on his schedule.
In a late-night Fox News interview, Trump acknowledged that soaring gasoline prices had hurt Republicans at the polls and were one of the negative consequences of the Iran war.
Vice President JD Vance addressed the midterm election results on Wednesday
Vance devoted long stretches of the campaign to supporting Republican candidates in the midterms
“I understand that, but I don’t agree with it. It’s a short-term problem for long-term gain… The gasoline prices were caused by Iran,” Trump said.
Vance had privately warned Trump against entering the war, although he largely avoided criticizing the decision publicly for most of the year.
He had asked Trump supporters to remain patient, portraying the conflict as something other than a “forever war” in the Middle East like the prolonged and unpopular campaigns in Iraq and Afghanistan.
IN CASE YOU MISSED IT: LA City Councilmember Nithya Raman Takes Lead Over Mayor Karen Bass
Secretary of State Marco Rubio had also urged caution in private before the United States went to war with Iran. After the operation failed to produce the swift outcome Trump had promised, Rubio likewise limited his public commentary.
On Wednesday, however, Vance offered his clearest public criticism yet, acknowledging the depth of frustration among Trump’s supporters over the decision.
The vice president referred to findings from several pollsters he trusts, saying the data showed that Trump voters turned out but delivered a serious warning to Republican leaders.
“I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this,” he wrote.
According to Vance, the polling indicated that Trump voters wanted the Iran conflict brought to an end, while demanding greater attention to the cost of living and persistent inflation.
Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio privately cautioned against the Iran war as they consider their political futures
Vice President JD Vance outlined what he believed Republicans got wrong during the midterm elections
Vance also pointed to polling suggesting that Trump voters wanted the administration to put “America first” and reconsider the country’s relationship with Israel.
Although Vance has been a prominent defender of Trump’s deportation agenda, he rejected the idea that granting “amnesty” to undocumented immigrants would solve the immigration issue.
“I’m open to changing how enforcement works—for example, by focusing more heavily on businesses that hire illegal labor. But anyone advocating amnesty is lying to you,” he said, warning that political commentators would inevitably try to “gaslight” voters on immigration.
Vance said he remained “hopeful” about the country’s future and urged frustrated Trump supporters not to disengage from politics after the Republican setbacks.
“To those who are angry and want to say, ‘I told you so’: You’re right—you did tell us so,” he wrote. “Put that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. And to those who are simply furious about the results, you should be. Let’s channel that anger into the work of saving our country.”

sources.news_title: JD Vance breaks silence on midterms humiliation and reveals 'the real reason we lost'
sources.text:
JD Vance breaks silence on midterms humiliation and reveals 'the real reason we lost'
Donald Trump's vice president has a lot to say after the midterm elections.
J.D. Vance has broken his silence for the first time since the Republican Party suffered humiliation in the midterm elections, claiming the "real reason we lost is obvious to everyone". In a post of just over 600 words on X, the US Vice President said he felt "negative" going into the ballot on Tuesday (November 3), after being "shocked" at a pollster telling him the Grand Old Party would lose the overall vote by 13 points against the Democrats.
Mr Vance said the same pollster found "a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry" and planning to vote for the Democrats. He added that when voters who abandoned the Republicans were asked what would win them back, they said the party should end the Iran war, focus on the cost of living and inflation, "put America first" and change the US's relationship with Israel.
Vance said: "Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results."
The Vice President, who was odds-on favourite to be the Republicans' nomination for the presidential election in November 2028, said in his statement: "The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night."
One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026. There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:1) End the war2) Focus on cost of living/inflation3) Put America First4) Change our relationship to IsraelOur voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.
— JD Vance (@JDVance) November 4, 2026
He concluded: "I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are p***** off and want to say, 'I told you so': you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview.
"To the people who are just p***** at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country."
Mr Vance's comments come as attention turns to the presidential election in two years. While he is the favourite to win the nomination, Mr Vance faces an uphill battle to distinguish himself from US President Donald Trump and maintain his support.
The Vice President would have to walk a fine line, with criticism of Mr Trump risking the President's anger and alienating his loyal supporters.
However, some Republicans, or voters who lean towards the GOP, may want to support a candidate who can admit to faults in the Trump administration and its agenda.
Mr Vance's analysis of the election drubbing drew swift praise from Mr Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr, who posted in response: "Every word of this. 💯💯💯".
Mr Trump himself addressed Mr Vance's statement, telling reporters later on Wednesday: "I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine."
While Mr Vance signalled he was prepared to change tack on Iran, the President defended his decision to go to war, telling Politico on Tuesday that he was convinced his decision to use military force against the country was "absolutely correct".
The Vice President's analysis also appeared to prepare for a row within his party over the mid-term losses. He paid particular attention to the White House's hardline approach to immigration and deployment of ICE agents.
He wrote in his post: "In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty.
"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you."
Mr Vance, who was Mr Trump's running mate in 2024, added: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.
"But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

sources.news_title: Vance's scathing Iran war postmortem puts potential 2028 GOP showdown in focus: 'Everyone knows why'
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance delivered a blunt assessment of Republicans' sweeping midterm losses Wednesday morning, pointing at the Iran war as the driving force behind the party's election-night defeats. 
"But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," said Vance on X.
"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost," said Vance. "And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
While President Donald Trump publicly addressed the results, which handed the Democratic Party control of the House and Senate come January, Vance remained quiet until posting a lengthy statement on X Wednesday. He argued that Republicans lost voters who backed the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 amid frustration over the war, rising costs and U.S. relations with Israel.
TRUMP DRAWS RED LINE AGAINST NEWLY EMPOWERED DEMOCRATS, VOWING IMMEDIATE VETOES
Vance's blunt assessment comes as speculation mounts over his own political future, with the vice president widely viewed as a potential 2028 Republican presidential contender. Vance has said he has not decided whether to run and planned to weigh his future after the midterms, raising fresh questions about how the GOP's sweeping losses could shape his White House ambitions.
"The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," said Vance.
The midterm elections dealt Republicans a crushing defeat, with Democrats flipping at least seven Senate seats and more than two dozen House districts to seize control of both chambers of Congress.
TRUMP ADMITS IRAN WAR CONTRIBUTED TO GOP MIDTERM LOSSES, INSISTS IT WAS NECESSARY
Vance's remarks mark a shift in his public assessment of the war's political consequences, after previously defending aspects of the administration's military campaign while expressing concerns about prolonged U.S. involvement overseas.
Beyond ending the war, Vance argued that Republicans must address the cost of living, recommit to an America First agenda and "change our relationship to Israel."
REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY
"In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you," he said.
Vance said he remained hopeful about the country's future and urged voters angry over the election results to channel their frustration into renewed political action.
"To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country," said Vance.
Vance said Republican analysts focused on the electorate’s "composition," whether it resembled the 2024 electorate and saw turnout holding up in many states. 
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
But a data analyst warned him that some Trump-Vance voters were angry and might vote Democratic, even if they still showed up. 
Vance said that forecast proved accurate, arguing that defections among 2024 Trump-Vance voters were a bigger problem than turnout. He also cited a pollster’s view that Republicans’ economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough late in the campaign.
Trump's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., reposted Vance's post with three red "100" emojis. 
Fox News Digital reached out to the vice president's office and the White House for comment.

sources.news_title: Vance blames Iran war for sweeping Republican midterm losses
sources.text:
Republicans are grappling with sweeping losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, which will give Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and create significant challenges for President Donald Trump's agenda.
Vice President JD Vance offered a candid assessment of the results in a post on X. He blamed the war in Iran for the Republican defeats, saying Trump reached a similar conclusion.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," he said. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."
Trump was asked about Vance's post during a beam-signing ceremony for the White House ballroom, which is under construction. It marked his first public remarks since the election, as republicans grapple with losing control of Congress.
He acknowledged that the war likely played a role in the midterm election results but said he would not have done anything differently.
“Well I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term and probably that’s probably it’s true,” Trump said.
“You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon," Trump said.
RELATED STORY | Trump deflects blame for Republican midterm losses as finger-pointing begins
Trump believes Republicans would have won if he were on the ballot, though he urged voters on the campaign trail to consider him on the ballot during his cross country campaign blitz ahead of Election Day as he sought to turn out his base. A White House official pointed to candidate quality.
“There was such love at those rallies it was incredible and we weren’t able to transfer the love to candidates,” he said.
Vance, meanwhile, argued that many voters who supported Republicans in 2024 switched to Democrats in the midterms. He also cited polling that indicated the cost of living and inflation were among voters' top concerns.
“The Vice President filed the first autopsy — it was the war. Others are writing a second that says it was candidates,” said Rob Burgess, a national republican strategist and CEO of Connector, Inc. “Both are looking at Washington. Neither is looking at the party. Our state parties, our recruiting, our message on gas, groceries and power bills…That’s where this was lost. Whoever rebuilds the institution is the nominee in 2028.”
Some conservatives, while acknowledging the results were not what they expected, believe their policy still stands.
“The conservative policy positions still resonate with the American public. We just didn't deliver the message, and we didn't deliver all of the things that we were supposed to have done,” said Doug Blair, a press manager with Heritage Action.
“I would argue that one of the things that Republicans and conservatives said that they would do is they would impact affordability issues. It's one of those things where Republicans came in on an agenda of making things more affordable, and they just weren't. It's the cost of groceries, gas, housing, healthcare. It's still up. We want to make sure that you know the American people are heard,” Blair added.
RELATED STORY | Voters elected governors to curb data centers. Lowering bills for gas and groceries is harder
But those economic issues will be a priority for Democrats, who are preparing to take control of Congress in January, according to House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. He pledged to work with Republicans on affordability issues.
"We've always made clear, as House Democrats, that we will find bipartisan common ground whenever and wherever possible in order to make life better for the American people," he told Scripps News.
Meanwhile, Democrats secured control of the Senate after pulling off surprise victories in traditionally Republican strongholds, including Texas and Kansas. Combined with their victory in the House, the results mark a major shift in power in Washington.
With Democrats controlling both chambers, Trump could face significant obstacles in advancing his legislative priorities during the final two years of his presidency.
While the President has suggested he could work with democrats on some items, the White House is also warning “In the final two years of his presidency, Democrats will try — and fail — to reverse everything President Trump has done” as Trump, who has already leaned into executive authority in his term thus far, has underscored veto power.
“I think that look I’ll get along probably with the democrats unless they want to be destructive but I have the power of the veto so if we don’t like what they’re doing or they’ve already called and they want to talk about things and that’s fine,” Trump said.
Democratic lawmakers are also expected to pursue investigations into the administration.
“If crazed Democrats want to abuse their power and politicize their process of investigations, subpoenas, and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers,” said a White House official.
Control of the Senate could also complicate Trump's ability to confirm future Supreme Court nominees if a vacancy arises, giving Democrats the power to block his selections.

By Rebecca Shabad | NBC News
Hours after Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance blamed his party’s losses on Americans’ frustration over the U.S. war with Iran, which has driven up oil prices at a time when costs are already high.
“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy post on X.
“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance wrote. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance added. “But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”
The vice president, a potential GOP 2028 presidential contender, cited an unnamed pollster whom he called “one of the smartest people I know in politics” who told Vance on Tuesday that in his polling, voters identified four top issues that they said Republicans would need to address to win back their support.
